summary: This local-news opinion piece argues that the city should invest substantially in real-time data systems for public transport, which it says would fix unreliable schedules and let authorities redeploy buses and trains on the fly. It cites benefits for commuters, the environment, accessibility, local businesses and tourism, and points to Taipei and Helsinki as models. It acknowledges financial, logistical and public-trust hurdles but concludes the long-term gains justify the outlay.
one_line: An opinion piece argues the city should invest in real-time data for public transport to improve reliability, air quality, inclusion and the economy.
key_facts: On October 3, 2023, a typical weekday morning saw commuters crowded on platforms looking at static timetables that did not match actual train movements.
Commuter Stephanie Rodriguez says she allocates an extra 30 minutes for her daily commute because buses and trains are unpredictable.

With real-time reporting of locations and passenger loads, transit authorities could redistribute resources on the fly, such as rerouting extra buses to a route with unexpected demand (the article's example is a congested morning on September 15, 2023).

On November 12, 2023, the city council's "Clean Air for All" summit highlighted decreased pollution as an advantage of efficient public transportation, since vehicles idling less use less fuel and emit fewer pollutants.
James Lee, a wheelchair user, said on September 30, 2023: "Knowing exactly when an accessible bus will arrive can be the difference between participating in the community and being left out."

At a summit on September 25, 2023, transportation economist Dr. Karen Simmons said an efficient system powered by real-time data can boost local businesses because people shop, dine and seek entertainment when they trust transport to be timely.
A study released on October 19, 2023, showed that visitors prioritize cities with accessible, reliable public transportation.
Taipei's smart bus system, rolled out in early 2023, has an app that alerts commuters to upcoming buses and potential seat availability.
Helsinki combines real-time data from all forms of public transportation into a unified system for seamless city-wide travel.
Equipping an entire fleet with GPS and sensors and building back-end data-processing systems is described as a major financial and logistical hurdle.
The article argues that long-term savings from reduced operational inefficiencies and a boosted local economy offset the initial outlay.
Public buy-in is a challenge: passengers must be convinced of the reliability and security of the systems managing their data, requiring outreach and education.
